1 Background
Electric propulsion systems for boats have gained attention in recent years due to their
potential to revolutionize the marine industry by offering a cleaner and sustainable alternative to
traditional gas and diesel engines. These systems most commonly utilize electric motors powered
by batteries, eliminating direct emissions of greenhouse gases and pollutants during operation of
the vessel. Research in this field predominantly focuses on improving battery technology to
enhance energy storage capacity and lifespan, optimizing motor design for higher efficiency, and
developing innovative charging infrastructure to support widespread adoption of these systems.
Additionally, many studies have explored the possible integration of renewable energy sources
such as solar and wind to further reduce environmental impact and to increase range. The
purpose of the unmanned boat is for it to be able to compete against other boats at high speeds
while optimizing the efficiency of the batteries and motor compared to weight. The boat is to
operate within the Elizabeth River, Virginia, where it will compete for the fastest time on a 2mile course. The primary mission is for the boat to be able to achieve at least 20 knots and
complete the race while remaining within the established safety limits.

outlines their process. To determine the initial design characteristics of the vessel, a parametric
analysis was conducted on high-speed boats, such as planing hulls, planing stepped hulls, and
catamaran stepped hulls. The following available data was collected.

To meet our length requirement, the hulls from the parametric analysis had to be scaled. Froude
scaling was used as shown in the table below. The scale factor λ was taken to be larger than one
as if our hull is in model scale. The scaling was done with a target LOA i.e. λ was calculated by
dividing the full-scale LOA by our target LOA. The analysis was done for target LOAs ranging
from 1.4m to 2.0m in 20 cm increments. A target LOA of 2.0 meters was chosen based on
displacement. The average displacement of the 1.8m scaling (the immediately smaller one) was
18 kg, whereas for the 2.0 meter scaling it was 25 kg. Considering machinery, especially the
batteries, a larger displacement is preferred. From the scaled data, our relevant range was found,
governed by speed, and it was found that the relevant hull types were stepped monohulls. It was
decided that our design would be a stepped monohull, and the other hull types and outliers were
removed from the dataset. Initial power estimations were completed using a variety of methods
and stated to be inaccurate. For this reason, and with the addition of a 30lb payload, the 2026
team undertook model testing to determine more accurate power estimates.

throughout this section that the “model” referred to is in fact the unmanned hull itself, not a scale
model.
2.2.1 Hull Preparation
The hull required significant modification to be suitable for model testing. Internal components
were designed and installed to create a strong and stable mating surface for the towing carriage
to mount to. Additionally, lines were added to the hull for the purpose of draft, trim, and wet area
verification. Figure 2 depicts the station lines added to the hull for underwater photo analysis.
Once the hull was properly marked and the required hardware was installed, it was ready to be
put into the tank and towed.
2.2.2 Test Procedure
Before collecting data, the instrumentation in the towing tank was calibrated and installed in the
model. The details of the calibration and installation processes are not within the scope of this
paper. However, it is important to note that the hull was outfitted with a pitch pivot (to allow a
dynamic trim angle to be reached naturally), a drag balance to measure resistance, a laser to
measure heave changes, and an inclinometer to measure static and dynamic trim angles.
The pitch pivot was installed longitudinally at the estimated LCG of the hull (approximately 1/3rd
of the LOA). The hull was then balanced-in-air to ensure that the LCG of the hull itself was in
line with the pitch pivot. The model was then ballasted to the freshwater displacement
corresponding to its saltwater displacement.
Although the pitch pivot was installed at the desired LCG, the pivot axis did not intersect
vertically with our estimated thrust axis. Therefore, a pitch moment correction had to be applied
before each run. Additionally, a thrust unload was required to account for the portion of upward
thrust that the hull would experience due to its dynamic trim angle.
The hull was towed at seven speeds, between 10 and 26 knots. The top speed of 26 knots does
not reflect that maximum speed intended for this hull but rather was a limitation set by the
towing tank staff to account for system, model, and test team safety. Since this was not a scale
model, full scale speeds were not scaled down for the model test. This led to a very high 44 ft/s
maximum towing speed.

2.2.3 Data Expansion and Analysis
Wetted surface areas were estimated from the underwater photos captured at each speed by
obtaining wet keel lengths and chine lengths and subtracting areas of flow separation after the
steps. The obtained wetted surface areas were used to non-dimensionalize the recorded data.
Then, freshwater viscous effects were subtracted out to obtain a residuary resistance coefficient.
Viscous effects in saltwater were estimated using the viscosity of saltwater, and then added back
in. The obtained total resistance coefficient in saltwater was then converted to a drag value using
saltwater density, to obtain the following speed-power curve for the hull in saltwater:

11170RPM, and 6.42Nm of torque, providing 247.27N of thrust, and a power efficiency of 59.30%
for one of two propulsors to be installed.
3

Overview of Build & Fabrication Processes

3.1 Propulsion and Powertrain
The propulsion system is designed and built from a combination of off-the-shelf parts and
custom mounts and adapters. The team faced difficulties finding parts designed for the size and
displacement of the boat, many were either too small or much too large. This resulted in
compromise on some aspects of the motors and surface drives including the rpm of the selected
motor, and the diameter of the propeller.
3.1.1 Motor Selection
To select a motor, the team undertook a spiral design process starting with initial research and
definition of the mission, followed by an initial design phase where multiple options were
proposed to estimate displacement and LCG. This allowed an accurate model test which
provided the necessary power curves to proceed to another round of initial design, where the
scope was narrowed to provide inputs for the propulsion algorithm described in section 2.3. This
algorithm provides the specific torque and rpm requirements necessary to select a motor. The
team selected two Maytech 11.5kW 8392 320KV Water cooled Motors.

The team determined that Arneson style surface drives were desired for maneuverability and

3.2 Batteries
The battery pack used to power this vessel is made up of 12 5S LiPo batteries with individual
capacities of 5200mAh. Each battery module contains five lithium-polymer cells connected in
series internally; this produces a nominal voltage of approximately 18.5V per battery (3.7V per
cell). The batteries are wired into six series pairs for a maximum total nominal voltage of 42V
(10S @ 4.2V/cell). The six pairs are wired in parallel to generate the total capacity of 31.2 Ah.
The batteries provide a maximum continuous discharge of 100C with surges of up to 125C,
meaning they can easily and safely handle our desired current draw. The current draw from the
batteries is 360 amps. The batteries are connected to a 500A fuse to prevent damage to our
system in case of failure in components or wiring. A wiring diagram of this system and the
batteries is shown in Figure16.
The batteries are attached to the hull using 3D printed brackets and Velcro. This will allow the
batteries to be easily removed and charged while also safely securing the batteries during
operation of the vessel.

3.3 Control System

pages.text:
13
The autonomous control system is powered by a CubePilot Cube Orange + flight controller. The
flight controller makes decisions based on the sensor data and position/attitude tracking done by
the GPS, IMU, and Compass. GPS waypoints are provided from the Mission Planner Ground
Control Station (GCS). The flight controller has a two-way telemetry connection with the GCS
over 2.4GHz ELRS using the MavLink protocol. The ELRS Transmitter communicates with the
GCS hosted on a nearby laptop over WiFi. The flight controller is tuned using the provided
parameters in Mission Planner and ArduPilot rover. Important parameters include battery
configuration, maximum steering angle, and maximum throttle.
3.4 Deck Cover
The deck cover of the boat is made of Dacron sail cloth because of its natural water resistance,
UV resistance, and high strength. However, on its own Dacron sailcloth is not entirely
waterproof, and water can pass through it at a slow rate. To address this concern, a resin was
applied to the sailcloth which helps to fill these gaps between the fiber. The Dacron is wrapped
around the hull and attached using epoxy to create a watertight barrier. To access the internal
components of the vessel, a drysuit zipper is attached to the Dacron to create a u-shaped flap.
This flap is waterproof and can be easily zipped and unzipped to provide quick access to the
internals of the boat.
3.5 Hull Structure - Ring Frames
Due to the high forces experienced in model testing, and the thin hull structure, it was
determined that the hull structure needed more strength. Ring frames were chosen as they
provide compressive strength without adding significant weight. Polycarbonate was chosen due
to its high compressive strength to weight ratio and ease of manufacturing with a CNC mill. The
spacing of the ring frames was determined by observing which points of the hull were under the
most stress in an FEA analysis of the hull under compressive lateral forces, to simulate the
pressure generated by the environment when in motion. After FEA analysis, the ring frames were
positioned such that a flat vertical face on the hull would be readily available for bonding the
ring frame to the hull, and dimensioned to follow the inner cross-section of the hull with an
offset width of 0.62 inches as depicted in Figure 17 and Figure 18.

Risks

The risks associated with this project varied from system to system, as well as with the vessel
operation itself. The challenge of starting a new autonomous unmanned team this year has led
the team to be further behind schedule than preferred. The team spent much of September to
December getting organized and completing initial research. This led in-depth research to be
pushed back to January and early February, with many parts being ordered in early March. As a
result, the team will only be able to test on the water twice.
In the power storage system, risk mainly comes from the high amperage the boat will be carrying
for its size, with an amperage of around 360 amps. Additionally, while the batteries are off-theshelf, modifications have been made to the connectors for the batteries to run in parallel with
each other to reach our desired capacity. To ensure safety of operation, high amperage connectors
and adequate gauge wire were used along with a battery cutoff switch and main fuse.
Control risks include telemetry loss, improper software configuration, and faulty wiring. All
these issues could be catastrophic and would require power termination. The wiring risks have
been minimized by fuses and thorough testing, and quality checks. Software and telemetry risks
have been reduced using bench testing and progressive levels of autonomy.
Stability was considered throughout the design. A weight study was conducted to ensure all the
machinery and their respective locations were chosen based on an optimal LCG of 66.7 cm
forward of the transom and VCG of 8.154 cm above the baseline. Tank testing contributed to
confirming these optimal values and calculations.
